question: Under the federal TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure (TRID) rule, how many business days before closing must a borrower generally receive the Closing Disclosure?
choice_d: There is no minimum timing requirement
explanation: Under 12 C.F.R. Section 1026.19(f), lenders must provide borrowers the Closing Disclosure at least three business days before consummation (closing) of most closed-end residential mortgage loans -- a federal requirement applicable nationwide, including New York transactions.

question: What does Section 8 of the federal Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA) generally prohibit?
choice_a: A borrower from ever refinancing their mortgage
choice_b: A seller from choosing their own title insurance company
choice_c: Kickbacks, referral fees, and unearned fees paid in exchange for the referral of real estate settlement service business
choice_d: A broker from ever charging any commission
explanation: RESPA Section 8 prohibits giving or accepting kickbacks, unearned fees, or referral fees tied to the referral of settlement service business (such as title insurance, mortgage services, or other closing-related services), protecting consumers from inflated settlement costs driven by improper referral incentives.
source_note: RESPA Section 8 (12 U.S.C. Section 2607) -- anti-kickback/referral-fee prohibition

question: What is the core consumer-protection purpose behind RESPA's disclosure and anti-kickback requirements?
choice_a: To guarantee every buyer the lowest possible sale price
choice_b: To eliminate the role of attorneys in real estate closings nationwide
choice_c: To require every closing to occur within 24 hours of contract signing
choice_d: To protect consumers from unnecessarily high settlement costs caused by referral arrangements that are not disclosed or that inflate costs without added value
explanation: RESPA's core purpose is protecting consumers from unnecessarily high settlement costs -- both through mandated cost disclosures and by prohibiting kickbacks/referral fees that can drive up costs without providing the consumer any corresponding benefit.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal RESPA policy rationale

question: If a brokerage refers clients to an affiliated title insurance company that it has an ownership interest in, what does RESPA generally require to lawfully take advantage of the affiliated business arrangement (AfBA) exception to the anti-kickback rule?
choice_a: Written disclosure of the affiliated business relationship to the client, along with confirmation the client is not required to use the affiliated provider
choice_b: No disclosure of any kind is ever required for an affiliated referral
choice_c: The brokerage must give the client a cash rebate equal to the referral's value
choice_d: The affiliated company must be based outside of New York State
explanation: RESPA's affiliated business arrangement exception generally requires written disclosure of the ownership/affiliated relationship to the client, along with confirming the client is free to use a different provider -- without proper disclosure, referring business to an affiliated company can otherwise implicate RESPA's Section 8 anti-kickback prohibition.
source_note: RESPA (12 U.S.C. Section 2607) -- affiliated business arrangement disclosure exception

question: How does an owner's title insurance policy differ from a lender's title insurance policy?
choice_a: They are functionally identical, and only one policy is ever issued per transaction
choice_b: An owner's policy protects the buyer's equity/ownership interest, while a lender's policy protects only the lender's security interest in the property up to the loan amount
choice_c: A lender's policy protects the buyer, while an owner's policy protects the lender
choice_d: Neither policy type exists in New York; only attorney title opinions are used
explanation: An owner's title insurance policy protects the buyer's equity and ownership interest in the property (typically for as long as the buyer or their heirs hold an interest), while a lender's policy protects only the lender's security interest, up to the loan amount, and does not protect the buyer's equity.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated real estate closing/title insurance curriculum content

question: A buyer's final walkthrough, typically conducted shortly before closing, is intended to:
choice_a: Replace the need for a home inspection entirely
choice_b: Allow the buyer to bring an entirely new list of demands unrelated to the contract
choice_c: Confirm the property's condition matches what was agreed to in the contract (including any negotiated repairs), not to serve as a new opportunity to renegotiate the deal or conduct a fresh inspection
choice_d: Formally transfer title to the buyer
explanation: The final walkthrough is meant to confirm the property is in the condition contractually promised -- including that any agreed-upon repairs were completed and no new damage occurred -- not to function as a fresh home inspection or a new round of negotiation.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated real estate closing-practice curriculum content

question: For a deed to effect a valid conveyance of title, what must generally occur beyond simply signing the document?
choice_a: Nothing further -- signature alone is legally sufficient to transfer title in all cases
choice_b: Publication of the deed in a local newspaper
choice_c: Approval from the local zoning board
choice_d: Delivery of the deed to the grantee (or their agent) with the intent that it take effect, and acceptance by the grantee
explanation: A valid conveyance generally requires not just execution (signing) of the deed but also delivery to the grantee with the grantor's intent that it take effect, and acceptance by the grantee -- a deed that is signed but never delivered does not transfer title.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general real property conveyancing curriculum content

question: In New York's customary attorney-driven closing process, what is the real estate broker's typical role at the actual closing table?
choice_a: The broker may attend but is not the party legally handling title examination, deed preparation, or the closing itself -- those functions are carried out by the parties' attorneys and the title company
choice_b: The broker is legally required to personally prepare and record the deed
choice_c: The broker replaces the need for either party to have an attorney present
choice_d: The broker has no role whatsoever and is legally barred from attending
explanation: Consistent with New York's attorney-driven closing custom and the limits on brokers practicing law, the broker's substantive legal role largely concludes once the contract is signed -- attorneys and the title company handle title examination, deed preparation, and the closing itself, though the broker may still attend to help coordinate and answer non-legal questions.
source_note: hedge: standard NY real estate closing-practice convention, consistent with DOS Legal Memorandum LI04's unauthorized-practice-of-law guidance

question: What form of funds are closing agents and title companies typically required to accept for the buyer's required closing funds, rather than a personal check?
choice_a: Cash only, with no other form accepted
choice_b: Certified funds, bank/cashier's checks, or wired funds
choice_c: A personal check is always acceptable regardless of amount
explanation: Closing funds are customarily required in a 'good funds' form -- certified checks, bank/cashier's checks, or wired funds -- rather than a personal check, to ensure the funds are actually available and reduce the risk of a bounced check disrupting the closing.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated real estate closing-practice convention ('good funds' requirement)

question: Once a transaction successfully closes, from what source is a broker's earned commission typically paid?
choice_a: Directly from the buyer's personal savings account, unrelated to the closing
choice_b: From the county clerk's recording office
choice_c: From the closing proceeds, disbursed at the closing table (or shortly after) pursuant to the listing/brokerage agreement
choice_d: From the broker's own escrow account, funded entirely by the broker
explanation: A broker's commission is typically disbursed from the closing proceeds at (or shortly after) closing, consistent with the terms of the listing/brokerage agreement -- distinct from the escrow deposit, which belongs to the principals until a proper disbursement event (see the broker's separate escrow obligations under 19 NYCRR Section 175.1).
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated real estate closing-practice convention

question: A current property survey is typically obtained or reviewed before closing primarily to:
choice_a: Determine the buyer's mortgage interest rate
choice_c: Satisfy New York's mansion tax filing requirement
choice_d: Confirm the property's boundaries, identify any encroachments, and verify the improvements are located as expected relative to the legal description
explanation: A survey helps confirm property boundaries, identify potential encroachments, and verify that structures/improvements match the legal description and any applicable setback requirements -- important due diligence before closing, particularly relevant to resolving any title exceptions.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated real estate closing-practice due diligence content

question: If a title search reveals an open mortgage or lien from a prior owner that was never satisfied of record, what must typically happen before or at closing?
choice_a: The lien must be paid off and a satisfaction/discharge recorded (or otherwise resolved) so that clear, marketable title can pass to the buyer
choice_b: The buyer automatically assumes personal liability for the old lien with no resolution required
choice_c: The broker must personally pay off the lien from commission proceeds
choice_d: The transaction is automatically void with no possibility of resolution
explanation: An unresolved prior lien is a title defect that must be cleared -- typically by paying it off from sale proceeds and recording a satisfaction/discharge -- before or at closing, so that the buyer receives marketable title free of that encumbrance.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated real estate closing/title curriculum content

question: Which of the following best reflects how mortgage recording tax (discussed earlier) and real estate transfer tax (discussed earlier) fit together at a typical New York residential closing?
choice_a: They are the same tax, collected only once regardless of whether a mortgage is involved
choice_b: They are distinct taxes imposed on different events -- transfer tax on the deed conveyance (customarily seller-paid) and mortgage recording tax on the new mortgage being recorded (customarily buyer-paid) -- and both are commonly itemized separately on the closing statement
choice_c: Only cash transactions are subject to either tax
choice_d: Neither tax appears on a New York closing statement
explanation: Transfer tax and mortgage recording tax are separate New York taxes tied to separate recorded instruments (the deed and the mortgage, respectively), customarily allocated to different parties (seller and buyer, respectively) and both commonly itemized as distinct line items on the closing statement.
source_note: NY Tax Law Article 11 (mortgage recording tax) and Article 31 (real estate transfer tax) -- applied to closing statement practice

question: A broker who is not an attorney is asked by a buyer client to explain, in detail, every legal implication of a title exception listed in the title report. What is the appropriate response?
choice_a: The broker should personally issue a legal opinion resolving the title exception
choice_b: The broker should simply tell the client to ignore the title report entirely
choice_c: The broker should refer the client to their attorney for a legal opinion on the title exception, rather than personally interpreting its legal significance
choice_d: The broker should refuse to discuss the existence of the title report at all
explanation: Interpreting the legal significance of a title exception is a legal opinion outside a broker's licensed scope of practice -- consistent with New York's unauthorized-practice-of-law limits, the broker should refer the client to their attorney rather than personally advising on the exception's legal implications.
source_note: hedge: standard professional-scope-of-practice principle, consistent with DOS Legal Memorandum LI04's unauthorized-practice-of-law guidance
